stem: Simplify without using a calculator: $\left({=bd}\right)^{\frac{1}{{=n}}}$. Give your answer as a fraction in simplest form.
solution: Write the decimal as a fraction in lowest terms: $\left({=bd}\right)^{\frac{1}{{=n}}}=\left({=bf}\right)^{\frac{1}{{=n}}}$.
Write the numerator and the denominator as powers with exponent ${=n}$: ${=bf}=\frac{{=p}^{{=n}}}{{=q}^{{=n}}}$.
A fraction with the same exponent on top and bottom is a power of a fraction: $\frac{{=p}^{{=n}}}{{=q}^{{=n}}}=\left({=t}\right)^{{=n}}$.
Substitute and multiply the exponents: ${=n}\times\frac{1}{{=n}}=1$, so $\left({=bf}\right)^{\frac{1}{{=n}}}=\left[\left({=t}\right)^{{=n}}\right]^{\frac{1}{{=n}}}=\left({=t}\right)^{1}={=t}$.
notes: The book's own standard exercise (0.25^(1/2), 0.81^(1/2), 0.008^(1/3)). The base is always (s/10)^n with s from 2 to 9 for n = 2 and 2 to 6 for n = 3, so it has exactly n decimal places and no trailing zero (0.04 ... 0.81, 0.008 ... 0.216) and the answer is s/10 in lowest terms (1/5, 3/10, 2/5, 1/2, 3/5, 7/10, 4/5, 9/10). 13 distinct instances. The solution follows ex2-4-2m: fraction, numerator and denominator as powers, [(p/q)^n]^(1/n). Decimal strings come from fixed(bf, n); the two constraints check that the reduced fraction really is p^n over q^n, so step 2 is true for every instance. The marker accepts any equivalent value; the stem asks for a fraction because that is the book's key.
